ACOM: Raw materials of all kinds: energy, metals and farm goods, reached through futures contracts rather than owning the goods themselves. Managers actively shift the mix, so it can act as a diversifier beside stocks and bonds, though commodity prices are famously jumpy.
AMGR: Growth stocks chosen under Islamic investing principles, led by technology at about half the fund, with industrial and health care companies behind it. The faith-based screen rules out banks and other interest-driven businesses, so it offers growth exposure that follows Sharia guidelines.
ANV: A note-like bet on NVIDIA stock built from derivatives rather than shares, designed to pay income while the stock holds up or rises. If NVIDIA falls hard, the fund can drop sharply too, and its steady payouts come with a ceiling on gains.
APDB: Large US stocks wrapped in a deep options cushion, set up each April to absorb a large share of a market fall over the following year. In exchange the upside is limited, so it is built for cautious investors who fear a big drop.
AUAU: Gold mining companies from around the world, the whole fund in materials stocks that dig and process the metal. Miners usually move more sharply than gold itself, so this swings harder than simply owning gold.
BBBL: Long-term corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest rung of investment grade, from industrial, utility and financial companies. They pay more interest than safer bonds because the companies are closer to a downgrade, and long maturities make the price sensitive to interest rate moves.
BDIV: Dividend-paying US companies picked for the ability to keep raising their payouts, spread across technology, banks, industrials and health care. It is built for income that grows over time, and because the managers choose the stocks, it leans on dividend growers rather than the highest yielders.
CBOO: Bitcoin with the roughest edges filed down: over each roughly one-year period starting in October, it seeks to protect against bitcoin's losses while following its gains only up to a cap. It is built for investors who want bitcoin exposure without the full stomach-churning ride.
CBTA: Bitcoin exposure that trades some safety for more upside room: over each roughly one-year period starting in April, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 20 percent while capping gains. It softens deep crashes but leaves investors carrying ordinary dips themselves.
CBXO: Bitcoin exposure with a safety net: over each roughly one-year period starting in October, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 10 percent while capping how much of bitcoin's rise it keeps. It suits people who want some bitcoin upside with a softer landing.
CBXY: Bitcoin paired with a partial shield: over each roughly one-year period starting in July, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 10 percent and follows gains only up to a cap. It offers a middle path between holding bitcoin outright and sitting out entirely.
CPHY: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier kind often called junk bonds, held indirectly through other bond funds. Instead of paying the interest out, it is structured to keep returns compounding inside the fund, which can help investors in taxable accounts.
DRMP: Companies in computer memory: makers of the chips and components that store data for phones, PCs and AI servers. The fund pairs that narrow chip bet with an income focus, so it aims for payouts alongside growth in one of tech's most cyclical corners.
EDGX: About 500 large US companies, technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, paired with call options the fund sells for income every week. The option sales pay regular income but give up some gains in strong rallies, so it is built more for payouts than growth.
FEMG: Mid-sized US growth companies, led by technology at a little over a third, with industrials and health care behind. Fidelity starts from the mid-cap growth group and tilts toward stocks its research likes most, aiming for stronger growth than a plain index fund.
FEMV: Mid-sized US companies that look inexpensive, spread fairly evenly across technology, industrials, banks and health care. Fidelity starts from the mid-cap value group, then tilts toward stocks its research favors, aiming to beat plain value funds while staying diversified.
FFF: One hundred US companies still run by their founders, heavily tilted to technology at well over half the fund. The idea is that founder-led firms think longer term and take bigger swings, so it is a growth bet with a distinctive selection rule.
FLDZ: US defense companies, mostly mid-sized and large industrial firms that supply the military. It is a focused bet on American defense spending, so it moves with government budgets and contracts rather than the wider stock market.
FRIZ: Companies with a record of paying steady or rising dividends, spread across technology, banks, health care and industrials. It is built to deliver income that can grow over time alongside stock gains, favoring reliable dividend growers over the biggest payouts.
FSEG: Small US growth companies, with health care the biggest slice at about 30 percent and technology close behind. Fidelity begins with the small-cap growth group and tilts toward its research favorites, so it offers fast-growing small firms with extra stock picking on top.
GMMA: An actively managed fund that shifts between US stocks and safer short-term government bonds as market conditions change. The idea is to join rising markets and step aside when things turn rough, so its mix can look very different from one season to the next.
GXDW: A fund of thematic funds: it holds other Global X ETFs picked by a momentum system that rotates toward the themes performing best. Technology, industrials and health care themes lead right now, but the mix changes as trends shift, adding a layer of active rotation.
HOYY: An options strategy built on a leveraged fund tied to Robinhood stock, designed to turn big price swings into regular income. It is a high-risk, short-term style trade: the leveraged base resets often and the options cap gains, so losses can pile up fast.
IBRN: Companies working on the brain and nervous system: drug makers and medical firms focused on diseases like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and depression. It is a narrow, focused bet on neuroscience, so it can swing hard on trial results and drug approvals.
JINT: Companies from developed countries outside the US, with banks the largest group at about a third of the fund. Managers use their own research signals to tilt toward stocks they expect to beat the pack, so it is an actively run core holding for international exposure.
JULI: Developed-market stocks outside the US, wrapped in options that absorb the first 15 percent of losses over a one-year period starting in July. Gains are left uncapped, which sets it apart from most buffer funds, though the cushion only counts at the end of the period.
KBUF: Chinese internet companies, reached through a sister fund plus options built to absorb 90 percent of a drop over the period ending in January 2027. In exchange for that deep cushion, gains are limited, so it is a defensive way to hold a volatile corner of China.
KMCA: South Korean manufacturers, split between industrial firms at about half the fund and technology companies, mostly chip and electronics makers. It is a concentrated bet on Korea's export factories, so it moves with global demand for chips, batteries and machinery.
LBO: Publicly traded private equity firms: the big buyout managers whose shares anyone can buy, making up nearly the whole fund. It offers a way to own the private equity business itself, collecting fees and deal profits, without locking money up for years.
MFVL: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, chosen by a value approach across technology, health care, consumer and banking stocks. It is a bet that underpriced big companies catch up over time, so it can lag when growth stocks are hot.
MYCO: Corporate bonds from many industries that all come due in 2035, so the fund behaves more like a single bond with a known end date. It suits savers aiming at a goal around that year, and its price still moves as interest rates change along the way.
MYHD: Riskier corporate bonds, known as high yield or junk bonds, that nearly all come due in 2030. Because the bonds mature together, it works like a single bond with a set end date, paying higher interest in exchange for more credit risk.
MYHE: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk-rated kind, bundled so that nearly all of them mature in 2031. The shared end date makes it act like one big bond: higher interest along the way, then principal back at the finish if issuers stay solvent.
OAIW: Companies tied to the OpenAI ecosystem: the chip makers, cloud providers and software firms that power or build on its AI tools. Technology is about two thirds of the fund, making it a focused bet on one company's orbit within the AI boom.
PGRI: Large growth companies from outside the US, led by technology at about a third and industrials close behind. Managers pick the stocks by hand, looking for fast growers in developed and emerging markets, so results depend heavily on their choices.
PJUS: A hand-picked basket of large US companies across industries, with technology the biggest slice at a little over a third. Managers choose the stocks instead of copying an index, aiming for a core holding that can do a bit better than the broad market.
PMAU: Large US stocks, the same broad mix as the S&P 500, wrapped in options that cushion the first chunk of a fall over a one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are capped, so it suits cautious investors who want stocks with a softer landing.
PMFB: The broad US stock market through S&P 500 companies, combined with options that absorb an opening slice of losses over the year starting in February. The trade-off is a cap on gains, making it a cautious way to stay invested in stocks.
PRXI: Stocks from countries outside the US, screened through a faith-based impact lens, with banks about a quarter of the fund and industrials and technology behind them. It gives international diversification with social screens applied, so some industries common abroad are left out.
QSOL: A fund that holds Solana, a cryptocurrency used on a fast blockchain network, rather than stocks or bonds. Most of the Solana is staked, meaning locked up to help run the network in exchange for rewards, which adds a little extra return on top of the coin's price moves.
RITA: Real estate investment trusts from developed countries that pass green building and social responsibility screens. It pays out property income like other real estate funds, but sets itself apart by favoring landlords with greener, better-run buildings.
RKNG: Stocks that individual traders crowd into most, drawn mainly from technology with some industrial and health care names mixed in. It is a bet on the crowd's favorite companies, so it chases popular momentum names and can move sharply.
SMYY: An options strategy on a leveraged fund tied to Super Micro Computer stock, built to convert the stock's wild swings into income payments. It is a risky short-term trade: leverage resets and option caps mean losses can mount quickly when the stock falls.
SQLT: Smaller US companies screened for quality: strong profits, steady earnings and clean balance sheets, spread across technology, industrials, health care and banks. It aims to keep the growth potential of small companies while skipping the shakiest ones, though small stocks still swing more than large ones.
TEC: Companies building or riding major technology shifts, mostly software, chips and internet firms, with technology about three quarters of the fund. It is an actively managed bet on change, so it leans into growth names across industries and will swing more than a plain tech fund.
TSSD: US-listed companies tied to national security: cybersecurity and software firms are about two thirds, with defense contractors and weapons makers making up the rest. It is a focused bet on defense and digital security spending, so it rises and falls with that one theme.
USVN: A single US government bond: the newest seven-year Treasury note, replaced with a fresh one as new notes are issued. It gives precise exposure to medium-term interest rates, rising when rates fall and dropping when they rise, with the safety of government backing.
WDIG: Companies that mine rare earths and other strategic metals, plus futures tied to those metals used in magnets, batteries and defense gear. It is a focused bet on a small, strategic corner of mining, so it can be volatile and driven by government policy.
WEPN: Defense contractors and rare earth miners, two areas governments treat as strategic, with technology and industrial names split fairly evenly. Options are sold against the stocks to add income, which can soften drops a little but also limits gains in strong runs.
XA: Cybersecurity companies that build artificial intelligence into their defenses: firms guarding networks, identities and cloud data. Technology is the entire fund, making it a narrow bet on digital security spending that can swing with the threat headlines of the moment.
